pages.title: 3 generations of women show how choices on having kids changed : NPR
pages.description: In one family, three generations of American women explore how choices around becoming mothers have changed at the same time the U.S. birth rate has dropped.
pages.text: 3 generations of women show how choices on having kids changed : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player 3 generations of women show how choices on having kids changed In one family, three generations of American women explore how choices around becoming mothers have changed at the same time the U.S. birth rate has dropped. 3 generations of women in one family show how choices on motherhood have changed January 28, 2026 5:00 AM ET By Sarah McCammon , Avery Keatley Caroline Brown (left) and Cynthia Briscoe Brown look at family photo album with their grandmother and mother Barbara Briscoe (seated) in Atlanta. Nicole Buchanan for NPR hide caption toggle caption i Nicole Buchanan for NPR American women today are having fewer children than their mothers and grandmothers did. They also have more opportunities and life choices. "I don't really feel like I got strong messages about what my life should look like beyond college graduation," said Caroline Brown, 33, of Charlotte, N.C.. "I was very much under the impression that the world was kind of my oyster." Like a growing number of younger women, she's unsure if she wants children. And she's not unusual; the U.S. birthrate now is about half of what it was in the 1960s. Caroline's grandmother, Barbara Briscoe, 93, says during her childbearing years, there wasn't a big question about what she was going to do with her life. These Are the Tactics That Kept Them Sane. As the world raced to rescue the trapped miners in a disaster that made international headlines, two psychologists were tasked with maintaining everyone's mental health. Chilean Minister of Mines Laurence Golborne holds a note from the miners while President Sebastián Piñera gives a speech during rescue operations. Miguel Soffia By Angela Posada-Swafford Published September 25, 2026 For Alex Vega, the morning of August 5, 2010 started off just like any other. He headed towards the San José mine in Chile’s Atacama region, then descended 2,100 feet into the ground to start his work. Suddenly, after four hours on the job, he and the other men working alongside him heard several high-pitched, whistling noises. Then came deeper, thunder-like sounds, followed by the rumbling noise of fast-flowing rocks. The mine had collapsed. The 33 miners were practically buried alive in an environment boasting 95°F heat, 98 percent humidity, and absolute darkness. “The initial thundering and the bangs we kept hearing meant enduring another psychological weight at the thought of the mountain sinking before rescuers reached us,” recalls Vega. The incident gained global media attention, with dozens of news organizations gathering outside the mine alongside the miners’ family, friends, and other onlookers—all of whom were looking to the Chilean government for answers.
